parts.transcript: Part 3. Luke & Millie on plastic buildings. Public disliked 1960s plastic houses because the idea of that sort of building as a home just didn't appeal - they didn't want to live in them (21 B). Engineers fixed wind by changing shape, but couldn't overcome plastic cracking in light then deforming when rain got in - effects of light and water (22 B). They agree to use academic journals in the library (23 A). Peterson's article: lacked illustrations/examples but was clearly organised and easy to understand (24 B). Structures: House of the Future 1957 - built to last, couldn't break it up (25 G strong); Wonderhouse 1964 - only a small model, design not implemented (26 E never built); spaceship houses 1968-78 - limited living area, low ceilings (27 B not much room); foam houses 1979-83 - built to show what computers could do at home (28 D promote technology); plastic exhibition hall - packed on a truck, inflated, reused (29 A easy to transport); New Zealand house - built from household/industrial waste (30 C recycled materials).

parts.title: Calotype photography in Britain and France
parts.transcript: Part 4. Lecture on calotype photography. Daguerreotype = first commercial process but copper made each photo expensive (31). William Talbot sought an alternative in the 1840s; he trained as an artist, his great interest was painting (32). He used paper instead of copper; calotype images were less sharp so more realistic (33). In France: 1851 a society for photographers was created with five members; Gustave Le Gray designed the first camera able to create enlargements (34). He made equipment lighter so it could be used outside the studio (35). He became famous because he wrote a popular series of books about the calotype process (36). Photography was thought more reliable than drawing and was used to record renovation work on historical buildings (37) in the 1850s. Debate remained on whether it was art; in the opinion of critics it could not compare to established art (38). Summary: photography was considered a science (39) reflecting 1850s culture; producing images on glass (40) made them last longer, leading to new techniques.
